# Truth Tables

The `truth-table` exercise type indicates that a code block will contain truth table
exercises. It has three variants: simple truth tables for one or more
formulas, validity truth tables (with a column for the double
turnstile), and partial truth tables with a single row.

## Simple Truth Tables

You can create simple truth table problems, checking to see if a formula is a
tautology, by specifying `variant=simple`, like so:

    :::truth-table{id="2.1" title="Exercise 2.1" variant=simple}
    Fill in the complete truth table.

    - ((P/\Q)\/R)<->((P\/R)/\(Q\/R))
    :::

`simple` is the default, so for simple truth tables you can leave out
the `variant` attribute.

The number `2.1` indicates the exercise id, and the formula is the one
for which you will be constructing a truth table. Note that the `- `
at the beginning of the formula, including a space before the formula,
is required. This produces:

:::truth-table{id="2.1"  title="Exercise 2.1" variant=simple}
Fill in the complete truth table.

- ((P/\Q)\/R)<->((P\/R)/\(Q\/R))
:::

You can also use a list of formulas, like so:

    :::truth-table{id="2.1" variant=simple}
    Fill in the truth tables for both formulas.

    - ((P/\Q)\/R)
    - ((P\/R)/\(Q\/R))
    :::

This example produces:

:::truth-table{id="2.1" variant=simple}
Fill in the truth tables for both formulas.
- ((P/\Q)\/R)
- ((P\/R)/\(Q\/R))
:::

Simple truth tables can be checked for correctness, and will be
considered correct when every row is filled in correctly. A problem can also be
solved by indicating a counterexample to tautology. In that case, only
the counterexample row has to be filled in correctly. A row is considered a
counterexample if *all* the formulas in the problem are false on that row.

## Validity Truth Tables

If your exercise specifies `variant=validity`, like so:

    :::truth-table{id="2.3" variant=validity}
    Determine if this argument is valid.

    P :|-: ((P/\Q)\/R)<->((P\/R)/\(Q\/R))
    :::

the result is a truth-table for checking the validity of an argument (in this
case, `P :|-: ((P/\Q)\/R)<->((P\/R)/\(Q\/R))`, where `:|-:` is just a stylized
way of typing out the turnstile). Note that formulas must be separated
from the turnstile by spaces. The above produces:

:::truth-table{id="2.3" variant=validity}
Determine if this argument is valid.
P :|-: ((P/\Q)\/R)<->((P\/R)/\(Q\/R))
:::

Validity truth-table problems can include comma-separated lists of formulas to
both the left and *right* of the turnstile. For example, 

    :::truth-table{id="2.4" variant=validity}
    Determine if both formulas on the right follow from those on the left.
    P,Q :|-: (P/\Q), (P\/R)/\(Q\/R)
    :::

produces:

:::truth-table{id="2.4" variant=validity}
Determine if both formulas on the right follow from those on the left.
P,Q :|-: (P/\Q), (P\/R)/\(Q\/R)
:::

Validity truth tables can be (by default) checked for correctness. A
table is correct when every row has been filled in, with rows that are
counterexamples to validity marked `F`, and rows that are not
counterexamples to validity marked `T`. A counterexample to validity
can also be provided directly by pressing the counterexample button,
selecting a counterexample row, and entering the truth values of the
relevant row. A row is considered a counterexample to validity only if
all the formulas to the left of the sequent are true, and *all* the
formulas to the right of the sequent are false.[^1]

[^1]: There's some arbitrariness in how we choose to think about the validity
of multi-conclusion arguments. This approach is the most natural from the point
of view of the sequent calculus.

## Partial Truth Tables

You can also create truth table problems that involve filling in a single row.
To do this, add the attribute `variant=partial`, like so:

    :::truth-table{id="2.5" variant=partial}
    - (P/\Q)
    - (P\/R)/\(Q\/R)
    :::

creating something like this:

:::truth-table{id="2.5" variant=partial}
- (P/\Q)
- (P\/R)/\(Q\/R)
:::

By default, the row is considered correct if it is filled in correctly, with
any assignment of truth values to the atoms. However by using givens (see
below), partial truth tables can be used to ask students to test for variety of
different properties.

## Feedback behavior

If `feedback=full` is specified, pressing the *Check* button will
color-code all cells as correct/incorrect and provide a count of
correct/incorrect cells. `feedback=terse` just tells the student if
the table is correct or not. (For truth tables, `check=cells`,
`check=terse`, and `check=off` are equivalent to `feedback=full`,
`feedback=terse`, and `feedback=none`, which is the way Carnap 1.0
handled feedback.)

## Additional attributes and options

#### Which cells to fill

The `fill` attribute determines what is asked of the student:

- `fill=all` (default) requires the student to fill in all cells.
- `fill=connectives` will populate the columns underneath the sentence
  letters/propositional variables; the student has to fill in the
  rest.
- `fill=main` requires the student to fill in only the truth values
  underneath the main connective(s).

The `fill` attribute does nothing in the `partial` variant.

#### How to grade a truth table

The `grading` attribute determines whether to give partial credit, or
only award full points for a completely correct table:

- `grading=all-or-nothing` (default) requires a completely correct
  table for submission (unless in exam mode) and full points.
- `grading=partial` awards points as a fraction of correct cells.

### Options

In addition to setting a custom point value or turning off submission by adding
`points=VALUE` and `submission="none"`, several
other options are available for truth tables. These are all set by
including them in the attribute `option="..."` with different options
separated by spaces.

- `autoAtoms` — pre-fill (give) the reference atom columns.
- `nodash` — draw empty cells blank instead of with a dash (`–`).
- `nocheck` — hide the Check button (same as `check="off"`).
- `nocounterexample` — hide the "Find counterexample" button and turn
  off the possibility to submit only a counterexample row as a solution.
- `hiddenGivens` — hide a partial table's givens.
- `strictGivens` — lock the seeded given cells, so the student
  cannot change the hints; applies to every variant.
- `double-turnstile` / `negated-double-turnstile` — head a validity table's
  turnstile column with `⊨` / `⊭` instead of `⊢` (display only).

So for example, 

    :::truth-table{id="2.6" variant=validity options="nodash nocounterexample"}
    P :|-: Q
    :::

generates:

:::truth-table{id="2.6" variant=validity options="nodash nocounterexample"}
P :|-: Q
:::

The `immutable` option (Carnap's whole-table *display* lock — distinct
from `strictGivens`) is recognized but not implemented yet.

#### Counterexamples

There are also a number of options that affect what counts as a counterexample.
These are set using the `counterexample-to` attribute. The options are:

- `counterexample-to=validity` (and `counterexample-to=tautology`)
  will ask for a counterexample in which all formulas are false.
- `counterexample-to=equivalence` asks for a row in which two formulas have different truth values.
- `counterexample-to=inconsistency` (and
  `counterexample-to=contradiction`) asks for a situation in which all
  formulas are true.

In the case of `simple` truth tables, these apply to all formulas. In
the case of `validity` truth tables, a counterexample is a situation
in which the formulas to the left of the turnstile are all true, and
the ones to the right of the turnstile have the counterexample
property. Hence, a validity problem in which the counterexample is
`equivalence` is basically using a truth table to test whether the
formulas to the right of the turnstile are equivalent "under the
assumption" that the formulas to the left of the turnstile are true.

Here's an example of a truth table looking for a counterexample to the
equivalence of two formulas

    :::truth-table{id="2.7" counterexample-to="equivalence"}
    - P<->Q
    - P->Q
    :::

which produces:

:::truth-table{id="2.7" counterexample-to="equivalence"}
- P<->Q
- P->Q
:::


#### Givens

It is also possible to give a "partial solution" to a truth table problem, in
which the truth table is partly filled in, and the student needs either to
complete it or correct it. To pre-populate simple and validity tables with
"givens" in this way, write the truth table you want, preceded by the bar
character `|`, after the problem. Fill the reference columns to the
left to determine which rows to fill. A period "." indicates a cell
the student has to fill. Cells for multiple formulas are also
separated by "|". So, 

    :::truth-table{id="2.9" variant=simple}
    - P
    - P \/~P
    T | . | T . F T
    F | . | F . T F
    :::

generates

:::truth-table{id="2.9" variant=simple}
- P
- P \/~P
T| . | T . F T
F| . | F . T F
:::

You do not have to provide every row, but the rows you provide have to
be filled in entirely.

If you wish to make the givens you assign immutable
(to clarify that they are a hint, rather than something that needs to
be corrected), you can use the `strictGivens` option. 

Givens behave similarly for partial truth tables. Here, you do not
have to provide truth values in the reference columns but can use the
wildcard "." instead. For example, 

    :::truth-table{id="2.10" variant=partial}
    - P \/~P
    . | F . T F
    :::

will produce:

:::truth-table{id="2.10" variant=partial}
- P \/~P
. | F . T F
:::

If a partial truth table is constructed with givens, then a solution
will only be accepted if it is "consistent" with the givens. So in the above
case, the only acceptable solution will be one that assigns `T` to `P`. The
givens can be hidden, using `hiddenGivens` (if you want to, for example, ask
students to make a sentence true and you want them to figure out the relation
between the truth of a sentence and the truth value of the main
connective). With hidden givens, it makes sense to provide mutiple
possible rows that are accepted as solutions.

A partial row constrained by a grid is graded all-or-nothing even
under `grading="partial"`; an unconstrained partial row is an
ordinary fill that can earn per-cell credit.


**Not implemented??**

If you wish to hide some givens, but not others, you can use a colon to
separate the sentences that will have visible truth values from those that will
not. For example, you can write

    ~~~{.TruthTable .Partial options="hiddenGivens"}
    2.11 Q : Q->P
    |    T   TT -
    ~~~

to create a problem in which the student must make `Q->P` true under the
assumption that `Q` is true. The result is like this:

~~~{.TruthTable .Partial options="hiddenGivens"}
2.11 Q : Q->P
|    T   TT -
~~~

so this can also be used to create problems in which students are responsible
for filling in a certain row of the truth table.

Finally, if more than one row of givens is provided to a partial truth table,
then any solution which is compatible with *any one* of the rows will be
accepted. So for example, you can write:

    :::truth-table{id="2.12" variant=partial options="hiddenGivens"}
    - P/\Q
    - P\/Q
    . . | . T . | . F .
    . . | . F . | . T .
    :::

In order to ask students to provide a row that witnesses the inequivalence of
these two sentences. The result will be:

:::truth-table{id="2.12" variant=partial options="hiddenGivens"}
- P/\Q
- P\/Q
. . | . T . | . F .
. . | . F . | . T .
:::

#### Custom Marks

The marks for truth and falsity can be configured to something other than the
usual `T` and `F` by setting the `falseMark` and `trueMark` attributes. So for
example 

    :::truth-table{id="2.13" variant=validity trueMark="1" falseMark="0"}
    P,Q:|-:P/\Q
    :::

will produce

:::truth-table{id="2.13" variant=validity trueMark="1" falseMark="0"}
P,Q:|-:P/\Q
:::

The handling of givens remains the same in the presence of a configured
`falseMark` or `trueMark` attribute. So,for example

    :::truth-table{id="2.14" variant=validity trueMark="1" falseMark="0"}
    P, Q :|-: P/\Q
    T T | T | T | . . .
    T F | T | F | . . .
    F T | F | T | . . .
    F F | F | F | . . .
    :::

will produce

:::truth-table{id="2.14" variant=validity trueMark="1" falseMark="0"}
P, Q :|-: P/\Q
T T | T | T | . . .
T F | T | F | . . .
F T | F | T | . . .
F F | F | F | . . .
:::

(The `turnstilemark` attribute is recognized but not implemented yet.)


** Systems not yet implemented**

#### Systems

The way that formulas are parsed and displayed can also be customized. This is
done by setting the `system` attribute to indicate which formal system you are
drawing your syntax from. So for example, 

    ~~~{.TruthTable .Simple system="LogicBookSD"}
    2.8 A > B & C
    ~~~

will generate:

~~~{.TruthTable .Simple system="LogicBookSD"}
2.8 A > B & C
~~~

The available systems are: `prop` `montagueSC` `LogicBookSD` `LogicBookSDPlus`
`hausmanSL` `howardSnyderSL` `ichikawaJenkinsSL` `hausmanSL` `magnusSL`
`magnusSLPlus` `thomasBolducAndZachTFL` `thomasBolducAndZachTFL2019`
`tomassiPL` and `hardegreeSL`.
